title: Unit Economics and Playbooks for Global Scale
description: Master the frameworks for evaluating international market entry, localization tradeoffs, and maintaining unit economics at scale.

interactions.prompt: Which metric best indicates whether a SaaS company can profitably scale into a new international market?

options.text: Total addressable market size in the target country
Localized LTV:CAC ratio after adjusting for market-specific costs
Number of inbound leads from that geography
Competitor revenue in the target market

interactions.teachingPreamble: When Spotify expanded from Sweden to 60+ markets, they discovered that global TAM was misleading  -  what mattered was whether localized customer acquisition costs and lifetime values made each market independently viable. A scaling playbook starts with unit economics, not market size. The localized LTV:CAC ratio accounts for translation costs, local payment processing, regulatory compliance, and region-specific churn rates.

interactions.prompt: A B2B SaaS firm expanding to Germany sees: CAC €420 (vs. €280 US), LTV €2,100 (vs. €3,400 US), payback period 9 months (vs. 5 US), gross margin 71% (vs. 78% US). What's the most critical signal?

options.text: CAC is 50% higher, making the market unprofitable
LTV dropped 38% while CAC rose 50%, compressing LTV:CAC to 5:1
Gross margin erosion of 7 points signals localization cost drag
Payback period nearly doubled, threatening cash runway

interactions.prompt: Shopify used a 'land and expand' model entering Japan. What defines the 'land' phase in a scaling playbook?

options.text: Launch full product suite with local partnerships immediately
Enter with a narrow ICP and minimal viable localization
Hire a full local team before acquiring first customer
Replicate the home market playbook exactly as-is

interactions.teachingPreamble: Scaling playbooks typically follow a 'land, learn, expand' cadence. When Shopify entered Japan, they didn't localize everything  -  they started with a narrow ideal customer profile (English-comfortable D2C brands), validated product-market fit, then layered on Japanese-language support and local payment integrations. The 'land' phase deliberately constrains scope to test assumptions cheaply before committing heavy resources.

interactions.prompt: In international expansion, the '____' measures how much additional revenue each dollar of incremental investment in a new market generates, and it typically declines as you move past early adopters.

options.text: Marginal market efficiency ratio
Incremental revenue multiplier
Market expansion efficiency score
Capital efficiency ratio

interactions.prompt: Your fintech startup has $8M to expand internationally. Brazil offers 3x TAM but requires banking license (12-month timeline, $3M cost). Singapore offers 1.5x TAM with regulatory fast-track (3 months, $500K). You can only choose one now.

options.text: Brazil  -  larger TAM justifies the investment and timeline
Singapore  -  faster time-to-revenue preserves optionality for Brazil later
Split budget: $3M Brazil licensing now, $5M Singapore launch
Delay both and invest $8M in deepening home market penetration

interactions.prompt: Why do many companies see unit economics degrade during the 'messy middle' of international scaling, even when individual markets look profitable?

options.text: Exchange rate fluctuations eliminate all margin gains
Shared cost allocation across markets obscures true per-market profitability
Customers in new markets always have lower willingness to pay
International markets require 3x the sales headcount

interactions.teachingPreamble: When Uber scaled to 70+ countries, each market appeared viable in isolation. But the 'messy middle'  -  operating in 15-40 markets simultaneously  -  created hidden costs: duplicated engineering for localization, multi-region compliance teams, and management overhead that couldn't be cleanly allocated. Fully-loaded unit economics (including allocated shared costs like platform engineering and central ops) often tell a very different story than contribution-margin-only views.

interactions.prompt: A PLG SaaS company with 200K free users globally is building its first international scaling playbook. Rank these actions from first to last priority.

options.text: Hire regional sales teams in top 5 markets
Analyze user data to identify highest-conversion geographies
Build localized pricing and payment infrastructure for top markets
Localize product UI and support for the #1 identified market

interactions.prompt: Six months into your Singapore launch (performing at plan), the government introduces a new data sovereignty law requiring all customer data stored locally within 90 days. Compliance infrastructure costs $1.2M. What do you do?

options.text: Exit Singapore and redirect resources to another APAC market
Invest $1.2M  -  this infrastructure enables expansion across APAC
Negotiate a compliance extension and evaluate the market meanwhile
Pause new customer acquisition until you assess full regulatory trajectory

interactions.priorContext: Previously you chose Singapore over Brazil for its regulatory fast-track and faster time-to-revenue. Now a new data sovereignty regulation has emerged, changing the cost structure of your Singapore entry and testing whether the market still justifies investment.
